title: FENa: Prerenal Azotemia vs Acute Tubular Necrosis
summary: Follow sodium through a thirsty tubule and a broken one, calculate FENa from spot samples, and learn why diuretics make it lie — and when to switch to FEUrea.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 15 Hit 1 (core: FENa in oliguria), Trap 2 (validity limits) and the Figure 15 memory anchor. The reviewer’s “> 1% suggests ATN” is refined to the consensus bands (< 1% prerenal, 1–2% indeterminate, > 2% intrinsic); see register flag rv-fena-cutoff.

objectives: Calculate FENa from paired spot urine and plasma sodium and creatinine.
Interpret FENa bands in oliguric AKI and explain the physiology behind them.
Name the conditions, especially diuretics, that make FENa misleading, and the role of FEUrea.

scenes.title: Same creatinine, different kidneys
scenes.altText: Two patients with low urine output and the same rising creatinine (2.0 → 3.5 mg/dL). Patient 1 has had two days of vomiting. Patient 2 is recovering from septic shock. A question token: “Are the kidneys just under-filled, or are the tubules damaged?”

cues.text: Two patients are making very little urine, and both creatinines have risen from 2.0 to 3.5.
One has been vomiting for two days. The other is recovering from septic shock.
Are these kidneys just under-filled, or are the tubules damaged? One urine and blood test helps answer that.

scenes.title: Normal: tubules take sodium back
scenes.altText: A schematic tubule: six Na⁺ tokens are filtered in from the left; healthy tubule walls pull almost all of them back into the blood, and very little reaches the urine. A formula card then defines FENa as the share of filtered sodium that ends up in urine, calculated from one spot urine and one blood sample: FENa (%) = (urine Na × plasma creatinine) ÷ (plasma Na × urine creatinine) × 100. A worked example: urine Na 10, plasma creatinine 2.0, plasma Na 140, urine creatinine 100 → 0.14%.

cues.text: The glomerulus filters a huge amount of sodium every day. Healthy tubules take almost all of it back into the blood.
FENa, the fractional excretion of sodium, asks: of the sodium that was filtered, what percentage ended up in the urine?
You need one spot urine and one blood sample. FENa equals urine sodium times plasma creatinine, divided by plasma sodium times urine creatinine, times 100.
Example: urine sodium 10, plasma creatinine 2.0, plasma sodium 140, urine creatinine 100. Ten times two is 20; 140 times 100 is 14,000. 20 divided by 14,000, times 100, is about 0.14 percent.

props.label: FENa = % of filtered sodium that reaches the urine

props.title: FENa (%) = (U-Na × P-Cr) ÷ (P-Na × U-Cr) × 100
lines: One spot urine + one blood sample, taken together

scenes.title: What changes: thirsty tubules vs broken tubules
scenes.altText: Top tubule (prerenal): blood flow is low but the tubule is intact, and it grabs back almost every Na⁺ token — FENa < 1%. Bottom tubule (acute tubular necrosis): the damaged wall lets most Na⁺ tokens flow through into the urine — FENa > 2%. A range bar then shows < 1% prerenal, 1–2% indeterminate, > 2% intrinsic (such as ATN).

cues.text: In prerenal AKI the kidney is under-filled but the tubules are healthy. Sensing low volume, they hold on to sodium even harder. Little reaches the urine: FENa below 1 percent.
In acute tubular necrosis the tubule cells are damaged. They can’t take sodium back, so much more spills into the urine: FENa above 2 percent.
Example: urine sodium 60, plasma creatinine 4, plasma sodium 140, urine creatinine 40. 240 divided by 5,600, times 100, is about 4.3 percent.
Between 1 and 2 percent the result is indeterminate. Read the number with the clinical picture.

scenes.title: In the lab: when FENa lies
scenes.altText: A checklist card: collect spot urine and blood together; FENa is designed for oliguric AKI. A diuretic token pushes extra Na⁺ into the urine of a prerenal tubule, raising FENa above 1% even though the physiology is prerenal. Other confounders listed: non-oliguric AKI, myoglobinuria, radiocontrast, metabolic acidosis. A second card offers FEUrea, calculated the same way with urea: < 35% suggests prerenal and holds up better after diuretics. A small token: pooled FENa sensitivity about 64% and specificity about 71% in one systematic review.

cues.text: Collect the spot urine and the blood sample at about the same time. And remember FENa was built for patients with low urine output.
Diuretics are the biggest trap. They make the kidney dump sodium on purpose, so FENa often rises above 1 percent even when the problem is prerenal.
Non-oliguric AKI, myoglobin in the urine, radiocontrast and metabolic acidosis can also make FENa misleading.
After diuretics, many labs and clinicians use FEUrea instead: the same formula with urea. Below 35 percent suggests prerenal.
Even at its best, FENa is only moderately accurate. In one review it was about 64 percent sensitive and 71 percent specific.

scenes.title: Two classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “FENa 3% after furosemide = ATN” is crossed out → “Diuretics raise FENa; use FEUrea (< 35% = prerenal).” Trap card: “FENa 1.5% = ATN” is crossed out → “1–2% is indeterminate; ATN is usually > 2%.”

cues.text: Trap one: a patient who got furosemide has a FENa of 3 percent. That doesn’t prove ATN: the diuretic raised it. Check the FEUrea instead; below 35 percent points to prerenal.
Trap two: a FENa of 1.5 percent is not automatically ATN. Between 1 and 2 percent is indeterminate.
And a FENa below 1 percent only means prerenal in a patient with AKI and low urine output — healthy people can have a low FENa too.

props.title: ✗ “FENa 3% after furosemide = ATN.”
lines: ✓ Diuretics raise FENa → check FEUrea (< 35% = prerenal)

props.label: FENa < 1% means prerenal only in oliguric AKI

scenes.title: Thirsty tubules hold salt
scenes.altText: Memory aid: a thirsty cartoon tubule hugs its Na⁺ tokens (“< 1%: thirsty tubules hold salt”); a cracked tubule leaks them (“> 2%: broken tubules leak salt”); a diuretic tap forces salt out of a thirsty tubule (“diuretic = forced leak”). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: thirsty tubules hold salt; broken tubules leak salt. Under 1 percent, thirsty. Over 2, broken.
A diuretic forces even a thirsty tubule to leak.
Where it breaks: it only applies in oliguric AKI; 1 to 2 percent is a grey zone; and myoglobin, contrast and acidosis can mislead. FENa supports the diagnosis — it doesn’t make it alone.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Three tokens: “FENa = (U-Na × P-Cr) ÷ (P-Na × U-Cr) × 100”, “Oliguric AKI: < 1% prerenal · > 2% ATN · 1–2% grey”, “After diuretics: FEUrea < 35% = prerenal”.

cues.text: In oliguric AKI, a FENa below 1 percent suggests prerenal azotemia and above 2 percent suggests tubular damage, but diuretics raise FENa, so use FEUrea after diuretics.

explanation.what: Plain language: FENa tells you what share of the sodium the kidneys filtered was let go into the urine. Scientific terms: FENa (%) = (U-Na × P-Cr) ÷ (P-Na × U-Cr) × 100; in oliguric AKI, < 1% suggests prerenal azotemia, 1–2% is indeterminate, and > 2% suggests an intrinsic cause such as acute tubular necrosis.
explanation.why: In prerenal states the tubules are intact and, responding to low effective volume, reabsorb sodium avidly; in ATN injured tubules cannot reabsorb sodium, so more is excreted. Creatinine is used to correct for urine concentration, so the ratio reflects excretion relative to filtration.
explanation.measure: Paired spot urine and plasma sodium and creatinine, collected at about the same time. FEUrea (same formula with urea) < 35% suggests prerenal AKI and is less affected by diuretics.
explanation.differs: Prerenal (intact tubules, FENa < 1%) vs intrinsic/ATN (damaged tubules, FENa > 2%); FENa (diuretic-sensitive) vs FEUrea (more reliable after diuretics).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a FENa calculation, interpretation in an oliguric patient, the diuretic trap (switch to FEUrea), and the limits — non-oliguric AKI, myoglobinuria, contrast, metabolic acidosis.

comparisons.title: Prerenal vs ATN
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the tubules can still take sodium back.

comparisons.title: FENa vs FEUrea
comparisons.distinguisher: Whether the patient has had diuretics.

mnemonic.text: Thirsty tubules hold salt; broken tubules leak salt — and a diuretic forces a leak.
mnemonic.explanation: Under 1% the tubules are thirsty (prerenal) and holding sodium; over 2% they are broken (ATN) and leaking; a diuretic makes even a thirsty tubule leak.
mnemonic.limitation: Applies to oliguric AKI; 1–2% is indeterminate; myoglobinuria, radiocontrast, metabolic acidosis and non-oliguric AKI can mislead; FENa supports, never makes, the diagnosis alone.

analogyLimitations: The six-token tubule exaggerates proportions: in reality almost all filtered sodium is normally reabsorbed.
“Thirsty” and “broken” tubules are memory images, not histology.
Example patients and values are invented.
takeaway: In oliguric AKI, a FENa below 1 percent suggests prerenal azotemia and above 2 percent suggests tubular damage, but diuretics raise FENa, so use FEUrea after diuretics.

questions.stem: An oliguric patient has urine Na 20 mmol/L, urine creatinine 80 mg/dL, plasma Na 140 mmol/L and plasma creatinine 2.8 mg/dL. No diuretics were given. What is the FENa and its interpretation?

options.rationale: Incorrect. A factor-of-10 slip; the correct value is 0.5%.

options.text: Cannot be calculated without a 24-hour urine
options.rationale: Incorrect. FENa uses one spot urine and one blood sample; the urine volume cancels out.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure and rising creatinine received IV furosemide two hours ago. FENa is 2.4%. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: FENa is unreliable after a diuretic; a FEUrea would be more useful
options.rationale: Correct. Diuretics increase sodium excretion by design, raising FENa even in prerenal states; FEUrea is less affected.
Incorrect. The diuretic alone can push FENa above 2%.
Incorrect. A FENa of 2.4% would not point to prerenal; it simply can’t be read after a diuretic.
Incorrect. FENa does not diagnose obstruction; imaging does.

questions.stem: Why is FENa low in prerenal azotemia?

options.text: Intact tubules reabsorb sodium avidly in response to low effective blood volume
options.rationale: Correct. The tubules work normally and conserve sodium when perfusion is low.
Incorrect. Filtration falls but sodium is still filtered; reabsorption explains the low FENa.
Incorrect. Damaged tubules (ATN) leak sodium and raise FENa.
Incorrect. Creatinine is not significantly reabsorbed; it is used as the filtration reference.

claims.text: FENa < 1% suggests prerenal; 1–2% indeterminate; > 2% intrinsic (e.g. ATN); FEUrea < 35% prerenal, > 50% intrinsic.
Diuretics raise FENa even in prerenal states; FEUrea is more reliable after diuretics.
Non-oliguric AKI, myoglobinuria, radiocontrast and metabolic acidosis can make FENa misleading; pooled sensitivity ~0.64, specificity ~0.71.
FENa (%) = (U-Na × P-Cr) ÷ (P-Na × U-Cr) × 100 from paired spot samples.
claims.note: Follows from the definition (excreted ÷ filtered sodium with creatinine clearance as GFR), but no external source stating the formula was read; NCBI Bookshelf was blocked.

claims.text: Healthy people can have FENa < 1%, so the bands apply only in AKI with oliguria.
claims.note: Stated by the reviewer (Trap 2); the sources read note reduced reliability in non-oliguric AKI but do not state the normal value.
